title: The Mockingbird M for Self-Application
description: Define the Mockingbird combinator M = lambda a: a(a) and test it on combinators that accept functions as arguments.

steps.description: Define I, K, and the Mockingbird M = lambda a: a(a), which applies its argument a directly to itself.

steps.question: What do M(I)(42) and M(K)('a') evaluate to?
steps.answer: M(I) evaluates I(I), which returns I, so M(I)(42) is 42; M(K)('a') evaluates K(K)('a'), which discards 'a' and returns the function K.

steps.description: Evaluate M(I)(42) to get 42 and M(K)('a') to get the function K.
Note on lines 11-14 why M(double) would fail: double expects a number to multiply by 2, whereas M passes double to itself.
Step through M(I)(42) to see M call I(I) and apply the resulting identity function to 42.
